title: Computer Organization and Architecture
description: The evolution of computers and performance measures; computer organization and architecture, the von Neumann model and the instruction cycle; registers and number representation; the CPU, ALU, instruction formats and addressing modes; RISC, CISC and parallel processing; pipelining and its hazards; and the memory hierarchy, RAM, ROM and cache. Built from the Ibadan Distance Learning course material for CSC 313 (Units 1 to 13).

topics.title: Computer Evolution and Performance
topics.summary: Computers developed from the Z1, ENIAC and EDSAC through mainframes, minicomputers and microprocessors to parallel machines and grids. Performance is measured by clock rate, CPI, MIPS, MFLOPS and CPU time, none of which alone defines a machine's performance.
subtopics: History: Z1, ENIAC, EDVAC, EDSAC, UNIVAC, IBM 360, PDP-8, Intel 4004
Architectural styles: CISC and RISC; scale of integration
Clock rate, CPI and CPU time

topics.title: Organization, Architecture and the Instruction Cycle
topics.summary: Architecture is the set of attributes visible to the programmer; organization is the operational units that realise it. A von Neumann computer stores data and instructions in one memory and executes instructions in sequence through fetch and execute cycles, built from logic gates.
subtopics: Basic functions and the four structural components
The instruction fetch and execute cycle
Logic gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR

topics.title: Registers and Number Representation
topics.summary: Registers hold the data and addresses the CPU uses immediately, and perform fetch, decode and execute. Numbers are held in binary, octal and hexadecimal, and signed integers as sign-magnitude, one's complement or two's complement, with real numbers in fixed or floating point.
subtopics: Binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal conversion

topics.title: The CPU, ALU, Instruction Formats and Addressing Modes
topics.summary: The CPU is a processor unit (ALU and registers) plus a control unit, which may be hardwired or microprogrammed. Instructions have opcode, address and mode fields in zero-, one-, two- or three-address formats, and addressing modes specify how the operand is found.
subtopics: The control unit: hardwired and microprogrammed
ALU design from adders and multiplexers
Zero-, one-, two- and three-address instructions

topics.title: RISC, CISC and Parallel Processing
topics.summary: CISC machines offer many complex instructions and addressing modes; RISC machines use few simple, fixed-length instructions executed in registers with hardwired control. Parallel processing runs parts of a task on several processors, classified by Flynn and limited by Amdahl's law.
subtopics: RISC characteristics; Berkeley RISC I; register windows
Need for parallel processing; programs, processes and threads
Flynn's taxonomy: SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD, SPMD

topics.title: Pipelining and Pipeline Hazards
topics.summary: Pipelining overlaps the stages of successive instructions like an assembly line; the RISC pipeline has five stages. Speedup approaches the number of stages, but structural, data and control hazards cause stalls, which forwarding and other techniques reduce.
subtopics: The five MIPS stages: IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB
Structural, data and control hazards; stalls and forwarding

topics.title: Memory Hierarchy and Cache
topics.summary: The memory hierarchy, from registers through cache and main memory to secondary storage, trades cost per bit against capacity and access time and rests on locality of reference. Memory is ROM (PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash) or RAM (SRAM, DRAM), and cache performance is measured by hit ratio.
subtopics: Levels and characteristics of the memory hierarchy
ROM types: mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, EAROM, flash
Locality of reference: temporal and spatial
